stem:
An unvaccinated 9-year-old has had a dry cough for 10 days. Over the last 3 days it has changed: severe bursts of coughing fits often end in an audible inspiratory 'whoop' and post-tussive vomiting. He is afebrile, otherwise well between episodes.

Which phase of his illness best fits this picture?

options.label: A
options.text: Catarrhal stage — most infectious, mild rhinorrhoea
options.explanation: The catarrhal stage gives a coryzal illness with mild cough; it precedes the inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting seen here.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Post-viral bronchial hyperreactivity gives a residual dry cough without the characteristic inspiratory whoop or vomiting.

options.label: C
options.text: Paroxysmal stage — follows the catarrhal stage
options.explanation: Severe coughing fits with an inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting define the paroxysmal stage, which follows a 1–2 week catarrhal phase and lasts about 1–2 weeks.

options.label: D
options.text: Convalescent stage — gradual recovery, cough fades over weeks
options.explanation: The convalescent phase (2–6 weeks, up to 3 months) is recovery: the cough tapers off, although a later viral infection can bring the paroxysms back.

options.label: E
options.text: Incubation period — no respiratory symptoms yet
options.explanation: Incubation is asymptomatic, lasting 7-10 days; the patient is already 10 days symptomatic with severe cough.

context: Pertussis runs through catarrhal (most infectious), paroxysmal (whoop and vomiting, about 1–2 weeks) and convalescent (2–6 weeks, up to 3 months) phases. Macrolides reduce infectivity but do little once toxin-driven paroxysms have begun.
